qs.whyOthersFail: The three distractors are real claims from other paragraphs in this column, but each is another party's argument, a rebuttal, or a proposal, not the thesis. More efficient electricity and warranties are "arguments worth hearing" from defenders of replacement. Late recycling is a rebuttal to that calculation. Ten-year spare parts are one of three rule proposals. The thesis is in "None of this difficulty is solved by lecturing individual shoppers about their choices" followed by a list of obligations for manufacturers.

qs.why: The author acknowledges that new appliances use less electricity, come with a warranty, and are made in factories whose safety can be inspected.
qs.whyOthersFail: The cost of repairing new appliances is never compared; small workshops actually disappear if everyone buys new; and recycled materials are not mentioned; recycling is instead said to come too late in the process.

qs.why: The usual comparison “counts the electricity of the new machine and ignores the metal, the plastic, and the shipping behind it”.
qs.whyOthersFail: All three are indeed in this column, but all three are actually arguments of the replacement side, not evidence that the calculation is skewed: repair kettles that can break again, new item warranties, and factories whose safety can be inspected are all mentioned as “arguments worth hearing”.

qs.why: Usulan intinya “Manufacturers should be obliged to sell spare parts at a fair price for ten years”.
qs.whyOthersFail: All three are reasonable obligations for manufacturers, but the text blocks them: what is requested are cheap spare parts for ten years, not a price reduction for new items; there is no proposal for manufacturers to do the repairs themselves; and regarding tax, what is requested is “the lower rate of tax” for repairs, not a higher rate for factories.

qs.why: “the price gap has narrowed” has the same meaning as the cost difference narrowing, so this claim is a direct paraphrase.
qs.whyOthersFail: “False” is incorrect because the direction of the change is not reversed; “Not stated” is incorrect because the effect of the rule is mentioned explicitly.

qs.why: The text's conclusion mentions the step literally: one roof, one year, one open report. So the purpose of this column is a small trial whose results are made public, not a large-scale installation.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options support the panels, so the blocker is in the author's own words: “a small, reversible first step: one roof” closes the proposal for the entire district. The author asks the school to act and never asks the district office to pay; the grant scheme is only mentioned as the reason “prices have dropped sharply”. Student meter reading appears as “the wider gain” after the panels are there, not as a request of this column.

qs.why: That sentence mentions two results since the grant scheme opened: prices dropped sharply and installers compete for small orders. The key states the same thing in other words.
qs.whyOthersFail: The text only says the grant scheme opened, not that the grant covers most of the costs. Installers are actually said to compete for small orders, so the other two options reverse the direction of that sentence: installer interest rose, and panel prices dropped sharply.

qs.why: The seven-year claim stands in one sentence: “Having compared three quotations myself, I am convinced the equipment would pay for itself within seven years.” The basis is the three price quotes that the author compared themselves.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options sound like reasonable evidence for the cost claim, so the blocker must be quoted. School bills are indeed discussed, but as an illustration of the problem in the first paragraph, not a return calculation. The figure of one-third of daytime demand is the author's claim about supply, not the district's estimate, and concerns power, not payback time. The installer's promise about next year's prices does not exist; the text only states prices have already dropped.

qs.why: The author answers the teacher's objection with one decisive sentence: “Yet that objection only measures the first year.” This means the teacher's calculation stops too early and misses subsequent savings.
qs.whyOthersFail: All options place the author opposite the teacher, so what chooses is the phrase “only measures the first year”. The teacher's objection contains two things (“solar panels are expensive, and thick cloud”) so it cannot be called just about clouds, and it is not a doubt about the roof either. The author does call it “a fair objection”, but that concession is not their position: “Another dry season of complaining about the bill would teach nobody anything” rejects delaying.

qs.why: This is a full paraphrase: “supply about a third of our daytime demand” has the same meaning as meeting about a third of the daytime electricity demand. So True.
qs.whyOthersFail: "False" is incorrect because no proposition is reversed. "Not stated" is incorrect because the number is clearly written in the second paragraph.

qs.why: The report's cause-and-effect chain ends in one finding: “the money earned from visitors was shared far less evenly than the team had expected.” What changed because of the fame is who holds the money.
qs.whyOthersFail: The three distractors are real findings from the second paragraph of this report, but each is one link in the chain, not the emphasis. The fivefold increase is the trigger at the start of the chain. The move of stalls to the back of the parking lot is a result of the rent increase. Two villages with daily booking limits are a comparison. The emphasis is stated itself: "the money earned from visitors was shared far less evenly than the team had expected". The third option is also in the form of a summary, but the booking limit is merely a comparison of two villages in that chain, not the finding brought by this report.

qs.why: The method is two things: interviewing 240 households and recording arrivals at every gate. The key mentions both in other words.
qs.whyOthersFail: Recording was done for a year and at every village gate, not one season at the waterfall above it. Rent increase is a finding, not a data source, and there is no stall owner's diary in this team's method.

qs.why: One sentence governs this comparison: in the two villages with booking limits, income rose more slowly but remained in the hands of local owners. Both elements, the rate and the owners, must both be correct.
qs.whyOthersFail: All options use the opening “their takings rose”, so the blocker is the symptom owner. Rent increases and the move of stalls to cheaper land happened in the nearby busy village (“rents along the main lane”), not in the two limited villages. And “grew more slowly” closes the option that equates the rate with the nearby village.

qs.why: The author mentions their own reason: the new figure “turns a boast into a test”, and the recommended figure is the share of spending that remains in the village after three months.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options use the form “makes a district show”, so the content of the figure determines it. The arrival count is actually rejected: “a district which counts only arrivals is measuring the wrong thing”. Rent increase appears as a chain of consequences, not a recommended figure, and the booking limit is a village rule, not a measure proposed by the report.

qs.why: The text says the four villages are within an hour's travel, so the claim "more than a day" directly contradicts it. The key is False.
qs.whyOthersFail: "True" is incorrect because the distance figure is reversed. "Not stated" is incorrect because the distance between villages is mentioned clearly in the first paragraph.

qs.why: The author states their position straightforwardly: both are not rivals but different goods, and the town needs both. The conclusion is to keep both, not to choose.
qs.whyOthersFail: The three distractors are indeed stated in other paragraphs of this article, but each is one point of comparison, not the main point. Subscription price is a cost advantage. The two-week-earlier print program is a cinema advantage in planning. Distractions at home are evidence for the attention argument. The main point reads "the two are not rivals but different goods, and the town needs both".

qs.why: The three details: open at four, 180 seats, one film per screening. The key unites all three in other words.
qs.whyOthersFail: The cinema opens at four, not noon, and only one film per screening. The number ninety is the number of audience members laughing together in the closing sentence, while the monthly package is a feature of streaming services.

qs.why: Paragraf dua memasangkan dua hal: bioskop “publishes a printed programme a fortnight ahead”, sementara katalog streaming “changes quietly, and titles vanish without warning”. Perencanaan itulah bedanya.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options are in the form of the same two-way contrast, so the blocker is the text phrase. The catalog is said to change silently and titles disappear, not increase every two weeks, and the word “without warning” closes the option that mentions a warning before titles are removed. The perpetrator also cannot be swapped: the one that prints the program two weeks early is the cinema.

qs.why: Kalimatnya menyebut sebab dan akibat sekaligus: film “competes with messages, cooking and a doorbell, so many viewers finish it in three sittings.” Gangguan memecah satu film menjadi beberapa duduk.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options use the pattern “watching at home tends to”, so the text signal chooses. Film length is never discussed; what is mentioned is sitting three times for the same film. Attention at home is actually stated to be divided, so “more closely” contradicts that sentence. Titles disappearing from the catalog are used for planning questions, not for home viewing habits.

qs.why: The text discusses the survival of the cinema but never mentions the source of its funds, let alone an annual grant from the district government. Such attribution does not exist, so Not stated.
qs.whyOthersFail: "True" requires a statement about a grant that does not exist. "False" is also incorrect because the text does not deny the existence of aid; it is just silent on that.

qs.why: The author praises what is delivered in front of the visitors (“what the show actually delivers is process”) and mentions one flaw: “The weakness is the labelling.”
qs.whyOthersFail: The three distractors are real statements from other paragraphs of this review, but each is a piece of evidence or a suggestion, not the overall verdict. The strongest room without finished cloth is evidence that what is presented is a process. The indigo panel whose creator is called a workshop is an example of labeling weakness. The suggestion to walk backward is a practical suggestion in the conclusion. The verdict reads "worth an hour of anyone's Saturday, though not for the reason the posters suggest".

qs.why: The best room is actually without finished cloth: there are copper stamps, a broken wax bowl, and two artisans working in front of visitors.
qs.whyOthersFail: The strongest room actually contains no finished cloth at all. The trade route only appears in the label paragraph of each object, and the bench in that room is used by two artisans working, not visitors trying to draw.

qs.why: For example, one object: an indigo panel from the north coast dated to within a ten-year range, but the maker is only referred to as a workshop. The date is neat, the person is missing.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options are in the form of exhibit-plus-flaw, so the text decides. The panel is actually “dated to within a decade”, so the example without a date contradicts the text. The copper stamp appears in the strongest room as a strength of the exhibit, not as a bad label, and the poster “promise treasures” is used in the opening regarding visitor expectations; the gallery does display cloth on the far wall.

qs.why: The advice is literal: “walk through the galleries backwards, starting with the makers and ending with the treasures.” Start with the artisans, end with the displayed cloth.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options use the same “start with … and finish with …” frame, so the direction and elements are what determine it. Opening with displayed cloth reverses the order he calls “backwards”. The trade route label is never the starting point or ending point he suggests; what he calls the end is “the treasures”, namely the cloth on the far wall.

qs.why: "The demonstration bench is free" means the same as visitors do not need to pay extra to watch it. So True.
qs.whyOthersFail: "False" is wrong because nothing is reversed. "Not stated" is wrong because the text mentions free explicitly.

qs.why: Suratnya menyebut maksudnya sendiri: “to describe a problem we can no longer solve with goodwill alone, and to propose a remedy that costs little”, lalu “we therefore submit two requests.”
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options use the same opening, so the second part is what is tested. Additional funding is rejected by the letter itself: “Nor do we seek additional funding.” Complaints about the office are also refuted: the office “has always answered our letters promptly”. The threat to quit does not exist; the text only reports “several have stopped coming” as a loss that has already occurred.

qs.why: Sacks are left at the market street corner, then torn by animals before being transported, so the trash returns to the river.
qs.whyOthersFail: Monday transport and weighing on the notice board are only proposed in paragraph three, so they have not happened yet. Sacks are taken to the market street corner, not the district office; that is where animals tear them before anyone transports them.

qs.why: The evidence is one sentence: “Volunteers who spent four hours on the bank watch that happen, and several have stopped coming.” That is the only figure showing volunteers are becoming reluctant.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options are facts that are indeed in the letter, so the blocker is the function of each fact. The number of sacks and the number of volunteers measure the scale of the work, not the decline in enthusiasm. Trash returning to the water is the damage seen by volunteers, which is the cause, not the evidence; what shows the effect on volunteers is “several have stopped coming”.

qs.why: Alasannya tertulis: “a public figure would keep both sides accountable.” Angka bulanan di papan pengumuman mengikat kelompok dan kantor sekaligus.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options use the framework “so that a public number …”, so the reason written in the letter is the differentiator. Work location selection is never discussed; the schedule is fixed every first Sunday. Correspondence is actually going well, so that number is not a substitute. And what is mentioned as the benefit is the accountability of two parties, not an inducement for volunteers.

qs.why: The text states that community service occurs on the first Sunday of every month, so "once a week" contradicts the written frequency.
qs.whyOthersFail: "True" is incorrect because the frequency was changed. "Not stated" is incorrect because the schedule is clearly mentioned in the opening sentence.

qs.why: The thesis is in the opening and closing sentences: keeping dance only for guests is “a tradition already halfway lost”, and the remedy is “one period a fortnight” in the schedule.
qs.whyOthersFail: The three distractors are actual numbers or proposals from other paragraphs in this column, but each is supporting material, not the central argument. The thirty out of thirty-four students who enjoyed the movements are actually used to dismiss indifference as the cause. The six students who had practiced outside of rehearsals are the measure of the problem. Forty minutes every two weeks is the cost of the remedy. The argument reads "A tradition kept only for visitors is a tradition already halfway lost".

qs.why: The two numbers in that sentence support the main idea: interest is high (30 out of 34) but opportunities are lacking (only 6 had ever practised outside a rehearsal), so the obstacle is time, not attitude.
qs.whyOthersFail: Six is the number who had practiced outside of rehearsals, not the number who liked the movements. Thirty is the number who liked the dance, not the number who joined the rehearsal for the delegation; the rehearsal was for the twenty best students. And practicing at home is never mentioned.

qs.why: The author mentions student difficulties as practical matters and details them: no slots in the schedule, no room after four o'clock, no paid teacher. Those three shortcomings are the evidence.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options are facts present in the text, so the blocker is the function of each fact. The number 30 out of 34 actually proves interest, and the sentence mentions the obstacle is not “indifference”. The department head's attitude appears in the final paragraph as an objection the author acknowledges, not a student difficulty, and the quota of twenty is a pattern the author rejects.

qs.why: One sentence provides the signal: “The dances survive on the stage and disappear from the corridors.” Performances mask the reality that on ordinary days, dance is not performed.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options use the form “they can …” and are equally plausible for an annual performance, so the text is the deciding factor. The quality of the twenty dancers is never assessed, and the interests of the delegation are never discussed. The last option directly contradicts “disappear from the corridors” and “only six had ever practised outside a rehearsal”.

qs.why: The proposal is indeed as follows: all classes get forty minutes with local dancers and the selection of twenty is removed. Therefore, True.
qs.whyOthersFail: "False" is incorrect because no proposition is reversed. "Not stated" is incorrect because the proposal is written in full in the final paragraph.

qs.why: Two short sentences decide it: “Equipment by itself altered very little. Conversation altered a great deal.” Contamination decreased in the ward visited by the explanatory officer.
qs.whyOthersFail: The three distractors are actual numbers from the second paragraph of this study, but each is one step in a chain of cause-and-effect, not the conclusion. The decrease from 31 to 9 percent is the measure of the result. Compost funding two additional rounds is a subsequent result. Material diverted to the landfill is the condition of the comparison ward. The conclusion is stated itself: "Equipment by itself altered very little. Conversation altered a great deal". The last option is in the form of a summary, but the sentence about the visible part is the author's interpretation in the conclusion, not what this study measured.

qs.why: The method involved weighing 1,200 sample bags every two weeks while simultaneously photographing their contents.
qs.whyOthersFail: What was weighed and photographed were 1,200 sample bags by researchers, not the entire bin by officers or incoming material by compost workers. Resident forms never existed; officer visits were the treatment being tested, not a data collection method.

qs.why: The fate of the materials differed: compost from the visited ward could be sold, whereas in the ward without visits “the yard diverted much of the material to landfill.”
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options use the frame “one ward's food waste …; the other's …”, so the blocker is the recorded treatment. Sample bags from both wards were weighed and photographed, so no ward was only photographed. No material was refused entry; what happened was it was diverted to the landfill. And additional rounds actually appeared in the visited ward, not as a differentiator of material direction.

qs.why: Both wards received the same bins; the only difference was the explanatory visit. Contamination dropped 31% → 9% in the visited ward and remained at about one-third in the ward that only received bins, so “Equipment by itself altered very little”.
qs.whyOthersFail: The 9 percent figure belongs to the visited ward, not the one without visits, so the second option reverses the data. The text never says the budget ran out in the bins so there was no funding for explanations; that is outside the text. And only the ward without visits diverted material to the landfill; the other ward sold the compost.

qs.why: The text is firm: only one ward received visits from trained officers, so the claim "both wards" directly contradicts it.
qs.whyOthersFail: "True" is incorrect because the scope was expanded from one to two. "Not stated" is incorrect because that difference is the core of the research design.

qs.why: The author mentions the basis himself: “the sensible advice depends on the traveller rather than on the accommodation”, then concludes that two imperfect options serve more visitors than one polished standard.
qs.whyOthersFail: The three distractors are indeed recorded in the second paragraph of this article, but each is one advantage or one disadvantage, not the main point. Four-fifths of the cost staying in town is a homestay advantage. Midnight guests who are not troublesome is a hotel advantage. Quality that differs from one lane to the next is a homestay disadvantage. The main point reads "the sensible advice depends on the traveller rather than on the accommodation" and "Two imperfect options, honestly described, serve more visitors than one polished standard".

qs.why: What hotels offer: locked doors, key cards, and breakfast at fixed times. The key mentions all three in other words.
qs.whyOthersFail: The one-third rate belongs to the homestay, not the hotel, and knowledge about dawn boats comes from the homestay host. Hotels do provide key cards, but breakfast is at a fixed time, not a choice of time.

qs.why: Kelebihan hotel disebut satu kali dan jelas: “Hotels, by contrast, win on predictability, because a guest arriving at midnight is never an inconvenience.”
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options use the form “a guest …” and all are accommodation advantages, so the text determines the owner. The description of guides charging too much comes from the homestay host, as does the four-fifths of money staying in town. The one-third rate also belongs to the homestay: hotels are called “duller and more expensive”.

qs.why: The risk is written in the sentence “Against that”: “standards vary sharply from one lane to the next, and a visitor who requires quiet may find none.”
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options are in the form “X, so Y” and all sound like risks of staying in a private home, so the text blocks them. The host's experience is used as an advantage, not a disadvantage, and fixed-time breakfast is a hotel feature. Money leaving town is directly refuted: “roughly four fifths of the fee stays in the town.”

qs.why: The text talks about accommodation choices but never mentions the month or season of arrival. There are no time figures, so Not stated.
qs.whyOthersFail: "True" requires seasonal data not in the text. "False" is also incorrect because the text does not deny that arrival pattern; it is silent.

qs.why: Penilaian akhirnya jelas: “Even with those faults, this is the most honest local film I have seen this year, and I recommend it warmly.”
qs.whyOthersFail: The three distractors are actual observations from other paragraphs of this review, but each is one specific compliment or complaint, not the overall verdict. Chalk numbers on the boat hull are an example of the film's strength. Two sequences of sewing nets are one structural flaw. Twelve minutes that could be discarded is an editing suggestion. The verdict reads "Even with those faults, this is the most honest local film I have seen this year, and I recommend it warmly".

qs.why: The decline in results is shown through three families who recorded catches over eleven months, the numbers written in chalk.
qs.whyOthersFail: The film is actually almost without narration, and buyers who determine prices were never interviewed; that absence is actually complained about by the author. The daughter appears in another scene, and the number eleven refers to eleven months of recording, not eleven years.

qs.why: The complaint is one sentence: music enters suddenly in the final reel and tells the audience how to feel about a scene that is already strong on its own.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options use the opening “it …” and all are reasonable music complaints, so the text blocks them. The net-sewing scene is criticized because it “add texture without adding meaning”, not because of the music. The repetition mentioned by the author is the repetition of the middle part of the film, not a musical theme. And because music only enters in the final reel, it does not override the catch tally.

qs.why: Two closing sentences: “The film declines to settle that dispute. It merely shows us that the argument is being had.” The debate is recorded, not decided.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options use the frame “the film shows a dispute …”, so the verb is what is tested. “Declines to settle” blocks disputes that have already been decided and also taking sides with the child. The idea of the fishing family disappearing is actually an assumption the film refutes through the scene where the child “rejects her father's advice and remains”.

qs.why: "Tighter edit ... gained considerable force" means the same as the film becoming stronger if it were shorter. Therefore, True.
qs.whyOthersFail: "False" is incorrect because nothing is reversed. "Not stated" is incorrect because the assessment of duration is written clearly.

qs.why: The author's proposal is one package: a daily limit of twelve hundred people with free tickets released earlier, because that “would treat both losses at once”.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options use the form “to urge …” and all are reasonable actions for an eroding site, so the text chooses. Stair repairs were never requested; what the conservator measured is used to justify restrictions. The lower temple appears as an alternative place for “those turned away”, so it is part of the proposal, not the intent. And fees are explicitly rejected: “I would go further and charge nothing at all.”

qs.why: What the conservator measured: stone eroded on the top steps, eleven millimeters in nine years.
qs.whyOthersFail: The original capacity of the stairs and the figure of four thousand visitors are used by the author as a comparison, not the result of the conservator's measurement. The time guides spend with each group was never measured; what was measured was the eleven-millimeter erosion on the top steps.

qs.why: The damage to the experience is written in one sentence: guides are urged to speed up groups, no one explains the carvings, and the visit “becomes a queue with a view”.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options are facts that truly exist in the text, so the blocker is what each fact proves. The number four thousand proves density, and eleven millimeters proves the loss of stone, not the loss of the meaning of the visit. The quiet lower temple is part of the diversion proposal, not evidence of damage.

qs.why: The reason is written straightforwardly: limits that work through price “excludes exactly the wrong people”, which is why the author chooses free tickets.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options use the opening “because a charge would …”, so the reason present in the text is the differentiator. The text does not claim fees fail to thin the crowds; the objection is about who gets filtered out. Where ticket money goes is never discussed, and the task of collecting money at the gate is also not mentioned; guides are only mentioned as being urged to speed up groups.

qs.why: The text says the lower temple is equally ancient, so the claim "much newer" reverses the written proposition.
qs.whyOthersFail: "True" is incorrect because the ages are swapped. "Not stated" is incorrect because the age of the lower temple is mentioned through the words "equally ancient".

qs.why: The report mentions the cause, not the numbers: audio grows because it survives while people move, accompanying bus journeys, turns in the kitchen, walks to tutoring.
qs.whyOthersFail: The three distractors are actual findings from the diaries reported here, but each is evidence or a result, not the emphasis. No one listening while sitting still is initial evidence for the cause. Expensive headphones that explain nothing is the elimination of competing explanations. The forty-minute episode is a lesson for producers in the closing paragraph. The emphasis is stated itself: "The interesting part is not the total but the reason", then "Audio grew because it survives movement".

qs.why: Their task was to write a two-week diary: what was heard and what activities were being done.
qs.whyOthersFail: The task was a two-week diary, not a weekly report or a monthly record. Travel time and video channels are indeed discussed in the findings section, but students were never asked to record both.

qs.why: The contrast is one sentence: video demands the eyes, whereas audio broadcasts only demand patience, so audio enters gaps that video cannot enter.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options are in the form of the same two-way contrast, so the actor and the demands are what is tested. Audio is actually what survives when listeners move (“almost nobody listened while sitting still”), so it is not audio that needs listeners to sit still. The actors also cannot be swapped: what demands the eyes is video. And expensive equipment is said to explain almost none of the difference.

qs.why: The two-week diary shows audio grows because “it survives movement” and teenagers choose forty-minute episodes “precisely because a journey lasts that long”, so episode length follows journey duration.
qs.whyOthersFail: The text says cutting episodes into three minutes “does not suit a listener with an hour to fill”, so the second option directly contradicts it. Ownership of expensive headphones “explained almost none of the difference”, so it is not a determinant of listening duration. And audio actually fills gaps that video cannot enter (“Where video demands the eyes”), not being defeated by video.

qs.why: Nine districts means more than eight, so this claim is a paraphrase of the written number and the key is True.
qs.whyOthersFail: "False" is incorrect because the number is not reversed. "Not stated" is incorrect because the number of districts is mentioned in the first paragraph.

qs.why: The first sentence of the letter states its purpose: asking for a decision on the directional signs before the next holiday season, and that season starts in six weeks.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options use the frame “to press the office to …”, so whichever request is actually written in the text is the differentiator. What is requested is not the publication of a survey, but a decision; the survey is only mentioned as not having arrived after four weeks. New funding is rejected by the letter itself: “none of which requires new funding.” And the guides do not ask to be relieved of duty; they ask for their boundaries of responsibility to be clarified.

qs.why: Perubahan Juni: jalur atas diperlebar, akibatnya pengunjung bisa sampai ruang kedua tanpa bertemu pemandu.
qs.whyOthersFail: The second sign at the fork is the letter's first proposal, so it does not exist yet. Additional patrols are never mentioned, and the 2019 route remains closed; it is only still written on the faded old sign.

qs.why: There is a single incident: last month two groups came in carrying torches after the last patrol left, and the floor of that room was wet limestone.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options take the form of incidents that would reasonably be used by a safety letter, so the text is what blocks them. The letter asserts “Nobody was hurt”, so no one slipped. No guides held anyone back; that is precisely the problem: the widened upper path causes visitors to pass through without meeting a guide. And April is the month the first letter was submitted, not the month people got lost.

qs.why: The third proposal is written separately: written confirmation that the association's duties end at the marked boundary.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options are requests that actually appear in the letter, so the blocker is their sequence number. The closing time stated as a number is the second proposal, and the written reply within two weeks is the closing request. New boundaries were never requested; the letter refers to the already marked boundary as the endpoint of responsibility.

qs.why: The text states the matter was submitted in April, while six weeks is the time remaining until the holiday season. The times are swapped, so False.
qs.whyOthersFail: "True" is wrong because the time figures are swapped. "Not stated" is wrong because the month of the first submission is clearly stated.

qs.why: The author's conclusion refuses to treat the two as rivals for the same household: livestock-farming families with people at home are given a digester, while families without both are given a cylinder.
qs.whyOthersFail: The three distractors are factual statements from the second paragraph of this column, but each represents only one side of a comparison, not the argument itself. Three-cow families cooking without cost is an advantage of biogas. Rising cylinder prices and flooded river paths are disadvantages of cylinders. Gas shrinking in cold months is a digester disadvantage. The argument reads "the village should stop presenting these options as rivals for the same household".

qs.why: Syaratnya tiga: digali, diisi tiap hari, dan diperbaiki di tempat.
qs.whyOthersFail: Delivery and igniting in minutes are characteristics of gas cylinders, not digesters. Three cows and a garden appear as the results of usage, not installation requirements, and there are neither daily fees nor annual repair visits in the text.

qs.why: The text pairs the two on the issue of supply: cylinder deliveries stop every time a river path floods, whereas the already built digester “is indifferent to the road”.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options use the same contrast frame “X, whereas Y”, so the direction of each claim is what is being tested. Delivery by boat is not in the text, and “indifferent to the road” rules out options that halt both. Digester gas decreases in cold months, not during floods, and cylinder prices here are said to have risen twice last year, not fallen.

qs.why: The author's assessment of the current scheme is firm: pushing one technology on everyone “guarantees that half the equipment will stand unused”.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options use the opener “it …” and all are reasonable evaluations of a village program, so the text blocks them. This scheme notably does not screen anyone: it offers one technology to all. Cylinder price increases are described as local market conditions, not a result of the scheme. And the text does not state this scheme is suitable for any particular group; half the equipment is predicted to stand unused.

qs.why: The text discusses who is suited to get a digester, but not once mentions who bears the installation costs. There is no attribution of funds, so Not stated.
qs.whyOthersFail: "True" requires a mention of subsidies that is absent. "False" is also wrong because the text does not deny the existence of financial assistance.

qs.why: The path the author offers is detailed: fund three part-time coordinators, publish an honest job description, and let the school offer those hours “as a genuine option”.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options use the frame “to call for …” and all are reasonable proposals regarding volunteer work, so the text blocks them. Shortening hours remains a duty, and the author says “compulsory schemes teach a lesson opposite to the intended one”. Certificates are precisely what he satirizes in the closing sentence. And he does not close the door on students: he wants the twelve volunteers who return next month.

qs.why: The six-year record supports his argument: volunteers who come through friends stay for eleven months, whereas those merely fulfilling compulsory hours stay for less than seven weeks.
qs.whyOthersFail: The eleven months belong to the group that came through friends, so the second option swaps the figures. The direction of the third option's comparison is the reverse of the record, and the school only appears as a distributor of compulsory hours. The number thirty is used for an example rota at the shelter, not for how long people stay.

qs.why: The hidden cost is mentioned in paragraph two: a shelter with thirty volunteers is reluctant to have to supervise, sign forms, and repeat instructions, and that is “paid in hours nobody counts”.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options are burdens actually mentioned in the text, so the blocker is whose burden it is. The number thirty is used to compare willing and unwilling volunteers, not as a condition for setting up rotas. Three part-time coordinators are the author's proposal, so they are the remedy, not the compulsory cost. Signatures appear in the example of the wrongly ingrained lesson, not as extra staff work.

qs.why: The sentence states the ingrained lesson: those told to sweep the yard for a signature learn that service is “a fee charged by adults, not a choice worth making”.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options use the frame “that helping …” and all are conceivable lessons, so the text cuts them off. Who values certificates is never evaluated. Volunteers through friends do stay eleven months, but that is a finding about retention length, not the ingrained lesson. And the shelter's dependence on school graduates is never claimed by the author.

qs.why: Six years means more than five, so this claim is a paraphrase of the written statement and the key is True.
qs.whyOthersFail: "False" is wrong because the duration is not reversed. "Not stated" is wrong because that working period is explicitly mentioned by the author.

qs.why: The consequence of the finding is written straightforwardly: the language is not dying but narrowing; it retains warmth and humor while losing formality.
qs.whyOthersFail: The three distractors are factual statements from other paragraphs of this report, but each represents a single line of data or a recommendation, rather than the core finding. Older people's habits are a single line in the usage patterns. Criticism of children's campaigns and the proposal for monthly meetings appear in the concluding paragraph as remedies. The core finding reads "the language is not so much dying as narrowing: it retains warmth and humour while losing formality".

qs.why: Empat situasinya: memarahi anak, menawar di pasar, berdoa, dan bercanda.
qs.whyOthersFail: The four activities asked about are scolding children, bargaining, praying, and joking. Forms, sermons, and school prizes appear in other sentences as domains of prestige, while greeting neighbors, singing, teaching, and reading announcements do not make the list.

qs.why: One finding was described as unexpected by the researchers: twelve- to seventeen-year-old students used the language almost exclusively for joking.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options are possible outcomes in this kind of survey, so the text is the blocker. Grandparents were reported to use the local language for all four activities, so it is not the national language when joking. Parents used it for scolding and bargaining, then switched precisely when praying, so their domains got mixed up. And one direct question was said to collect polite answers, rather than sharper ones.

qs.why: The pattern follows function, not age: 12–17 year-old students still use the language for joking, while official domains are gone, so the author concludes that the campaign targeting children missed the target and the opportunity for adults is what was lost.
qs.whyOthersFail: The imitation of grandparents' language is never discussed in this survey. There are no records of any children's campaign ever tried and failing in this district. And the last option reverses the finding: joking is actually the only domain still held by the youngest group (“almost exclusively for joking”).

qs.why: The text states that parents use the local language for bargaining and switch to the national language when praying, so this claim mixes up the domains.
qs.whyOthersFail: "True" is wrong because the activities are swapped. "Not stated" is wrong because the parents' habits are detailed in the second paragraph.

qs.why: The final evaluation is in the concluding sentence: this book knows the difference between a travel guide and a historical study, “which is why its faults are forgivable”, after its flaws are listed one by one.
qs.whyOthersFail: The three distractors are indeed stated elsewhere in this review, but each represents a single feature, a list of flaws, or a buying recommendation, rather than its overall evaluation. The four pages of history describe the book's structure. The dark photos and the index missing two mosques are specific details. Buying it before arriving is a practical suggestion. The evaluation reads "This one knows the difference, which is why its faults are forgivable".

qs.why: The maps work like this: one route per double-page spread, and the turns are drawn as seen by a pedestrian, not in a surveyor's style.
qs.whyOthersFail: The surveyor's method is precisely what is rejected; the turns are drawn as seen by a pedestrian. The routes are six, not four, and the fish market alley has a special margin note about hours when it cannot be passed. The fold-out map at the back is never mentioned.

qs.why: What marks the book as quickly outdated is a single flaw: the ship fares printed inside it were already wrong in July, prompting the author to suggest printing the month on the cover.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options are flaws actually reported by the review, so the blocker is which flaw changes over time. The gap-toothed index and dark photos remain equally flawed a year later, so neither is an issue of becoming outdated. The four-page history is not even a flaw: it is a choice praised as the opposite of other guides.

qs.why: The advice is clear: buy it before arrival and read it at home, because a paragraph about a warehouse leaning toward the sea rearranges the entire area for visitors.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options use the opening "read it …", so time and place are being tested. Reading it after the visit reverses the advice to “Read at home” which precedes the journey. The station kiosk is explicitly rejected: “purchase it before arrival rather than at the station kiosk”. And the ship fares are said to be already wrong, not changing every month.

qs.why: The history is only four pages and the rest is about streets, so this claim is an accurate paraphrase and the key is True.
qs.whyOthersFail: "False" is wrong because the comparison is not reversed. "Not stated" is wrong because the page proportions are clearly stated.

qs.why: The author rejects two explanations at once: “Something is occurring, but it is not a simple loss of patience”, and what has changed is “the cost of leaving”.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options use the frame “to show/ask …” and all represent reasonable attitudes in this debate, so the text is the blocker. The author does not say the change is exaggerated; he says something has genuinely changed, just not patience. He rejects clip restrictions himself: “I do not seek a ban.” And history and mathematics are used as examples of texts that are slow to reciprocate, not as the main subject.

qs.why: The survey results precisely support his thesis: reading ability has not dropped, what has changed is the willingness to persevere with new texts; this is about the cost of leaving, not about attention span.
qs.whyOthersFail: The survey calls them “no worse at reading”, so the second option reverses the result. The figure of leaving the text twice as often belongs to heavy clip viewers, not the group that watches very little. And the last option erases the core finding, because new texts are actually the ones most frequently abandoned.

qs.why: The contrast is built around the cost of leaving: novel chapters make leaving feel awkward, whereas videos offering replacements every three seconds make “staying an active decision”.
qs.whyOthersFail: Three options share the same first half, so their second halves are being tested. The direction must not be reversed: the awkward thing to leave behind is the novel, not the clip. And with clips, what requires an active decision is staying, not leaving, which is why staying does not happen automatically.

qs.why: Penulis memberi contohnya sendiri: beri tahu kelas bahwa empat halaman pertama sebuah novel sengaja lambat, “and many of them will hold on”.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options take the form of short commands to teachers and all sound plausible, so the text is the blocker. Replacing the novel and skipping the opening both eliminate that slow section, whereas the author actually asks for that section to be named first. Allowing students to close the text also contradicts his goal: “many of them will hold on”.

qs.why: The text mentions a two-hour video as an example, but never gives the number of hours spent watching clips per day. The quantity is not mentioned, so it is Not stated.
qs.whyOthersFail: "True" requires a daily figure that is missing. "False" is also wrong because the text does not dispute that figure; it simply does not measure it.

qs.why: The report's author formulates it thus: duty may bring someone in the first time, but “evidence of effect brings her back”; the group informed that their bags were reused came back at nearly twice the rate.
qs.whyOthersFail: The three distractors are actual statements from this experimental report, but each is a side result, methodological note, or budget proposal, rather than its conclusion. The message about shortcomings having no effect serves as a comparison. The similarity in age and occupation is the reason the result is not a coincidence. The reallocation of poster funds is in the final sentence. The conclusion reads "Duty may bring somebody in the first time; evidence of effect brings her back". The second option is also framed as a summary and is indeed written in the text, but it explains the first visit; this experiment tests the second visit.

qs.why: The first group received a thank-you note plus the information that their bag was used within nine days.
qs.whyOthersFail: The scarcity warning is the message for the second group, and the plain card with no additions is for the third group. The number nine refers to days, not weeks; sixteen weeks is the interval for measuring results.

qs.why: The results are sharply divided: sixteen weeks later, the first group returned at nearly twice the rate of the third group, whereas the scarcity message produced no measurable effect.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options take the form of comparisons among the same three groups, so the text's numbers are the blocker. Because the scarcity message raised nothing, the two messaging groups could not have both increased, and the scarcity group could not possibly be double. And the three groups clearly did not achieve equal results: the difference between the first and third groups was nearly double.

qs.why: The group told about their blood usage returned at nearly twice the rate, whereas the scarcity reminder had no effect; the conclusion is “Duty may bring somebody in the first time; evidence of effect brings her back”, so the duty poster speaks at the wrong moment.
qs.whyOthersFail: The scarcity reminder “produced no measurable effect at all”, so mentioning scarcity is not what makes the poster work. The nearly double figure belongs to the usage message group, not the poster. And duty does not drive newcomers away; the text explicitly states that duty can bring people in the first time.

qs.why: The text states that the three groups were similar in age and occupation, so the claim that they "differed sharply" reverses that statement.
qs.whyOthersFail: "True" is incorrect because the polarity is reversed. "Not stated" is incorrect because the similarity of the groups is mentioned to defend the results.

qs.why: The author states their position: the two villages “are buying different things and should admit it”; sponsors buy scale at the cost of editing, while dues-paying members buy control at the cost of reach.
qs.whyOthersFail: The three distractors are factual details from the second paragraph of this column, but each is a single point of comparison, not the main point. The three studios from the provincial capital are evidence of the sponsored festival's luxury. The six forms not performed since 2016 are the advantage of the dues-paying festival. The sentence about spectators preserving tradition is a concession for the sponsored village. The main point is that "the two villages are buying different things and should admit it".

qs.why: The money is used for rented sound systems, printed schedules, and three studios from the provincial capital.
qs.whyOthersFail: Volunteers, six local forms, and a long procession are characteristics of the dues-paying village. There are three paid studios, not two, and there are no dues collectors in the sponsored village; naming rights are the source of funds, not the expenditure.

qs.why: The advantages of the dues-paying festival are mentioned in the “Yet” sentence: the event includes six local forms that the sponsored village has not performed since 2016, including that long procession.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options use the opening “it …” and are all plausible advantages for a festival, so the text acts as the blocker. The four thousand spectators and three paid studios from the provincial capital belong to the sponsored village. The dues-paying festival's budget is actually about one-tenth, not ten times, and the event uses volunteers throughout the street.

qs.why: The word “editing” is explained by its examples: the long procession was considered by the sponsor to be “too slow for photographs” and six local forms were removed from the sponsored village's event.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options use the opening “sponsors quietly …”, so the meaning of “editing” is being tested. Paying for sound systems and printed schedules is the “scale and comfort” that sponsors buy, not the editing of the event. Leaving the program arrangement to the residents is a compromise the author proposes, which is the opposite of the sponsor's attitude. And the request to photograph banners is never mentioned in the text.

qs.why: "Used volunteers throughout" means the same as running without paid workers. Therefore, True.
qs.whyOthersFail: "False" is incorrect because no propositions were swapped. "Not stated" is incorrect because the use of volunteers is clearly mentioned.

qs.why: The letter states its purpose in the first paragraph: to describe a measurable problem and propose a specific remedy, then request two actions and one commitment.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options use the frame “to …” and are all reasonable steps for residents affected by dust, so the text acts as the blocker. Closing the second line is rejected by the letter itself: “we are not asking for the second line to be shut.” The factory engineer is mentioned as explaining the filter in April, so they were not ignored. And compensation for laundry racks was never requested.

qs.why: Two members recorded dust deposits on glass plates of the same type for eight weeks.
qs.whyOthersFail: What the two members did was record deposits on similar glass plates for eight weeks. The number ninety is the number of households represented by the committee, wind direction is only mentioned as strengthening in the afternoon, and there is no daily photography.

qs.why: What points to the source is the comparison of two similar plates: the one closest to the factory fence collected about five times the dust of the plate at the far end of the street.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options are findings that actually exist in the letter, so the blocker is what each finding proves. Dust settling every workday proves there is dust, not its origin. Moved laundry racks and closed school windows prove the impact. Only the difference between the plates points to the direction the dust comes from.

qs.why: The closing sentence mentions the reason: if the numbers go down, the neighbors will know; if not, both parties still have a shared record instead of “an argument about impressions”.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options use the opening “to …” and are all reasonable reasons to publish the numbers, so the text acts as the blocker. The committee never compared its accuracy with the factory's measurements. School windows are mentioned as a consequence of the dust, not the purpose of publication. And the cost of filters is never discussed in this letter.

qs.why: The letter mentions the problem has existed since the second saw line opened in March, so the claim about the first line swaps the culprit.
qs.whyOthersFail: "True" is incorrect because the lines were swapped. "Not stated" is incorrect because the start of the problem is clearly mentioned in the second paragraph.

qs.why: The author's proposal is detailed: accept the coach for one afternoon, keep the parents on the other afternoon, and ask the coach to teach them for an hour a month.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options use the frame “take/turn the visiting coach …”, so the scope is what is being tested. Taking the coach for a full week means meeting the district's requirement that parents step back, and that requirement is “the whole difficulty”. The coach's working hours were never requested to be extended. And refusing the offer is only suggested as a backup, “if the district insists that its coach works alone”.

qs.why: There is only one condition: the parents who currently run the training must step back.
qs.whyOthersFail: The only condition mentioned is that the parents who currently run the training must step back. Costs were never mentioned, one hour of training for parents is the author's proposal, and four to six o'clock is a description of the coach's arrival, not a condition.

qs.why: The example used by the author is one: when rain canceled training for three weeks in February, it was two fathers who called every family.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options are events in a small club that are equally plausible, so the text acts as the blocker. February was actually the month training was canceled for three weeks, so it is not the month children kept coming. The visiting coach was not yet working at the club, and the text mentions he arrives at four and leaves at six. A child who stopped talking to their sibling is an example of something the two-hour coach would not have time to see, not an event that was reported.

qs.why: The sentence mentions the distinguished result: the district schedule, while professional, “produces attendance rather than attachment”; children come, but a sense of being waited for is not born from a schedule.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options use the opening “a timetable …” and are all reasonable claims about official schedules, so the text acts as the blocker. Attendance recording is never discussed. Increased attendance due to a professional coach is also not claimed; what is claimed is attendance without attachment. And parents are described as the opposite of number-keepers: their strength is “they are permanent”.

qs.why: Penulis mengakui pelatih tamu memperbaiki teknik, jadi klaim ini parafrasa pengakuan itu dan kuncinya True.
qs.whyOthersFail: "False" is incorrect because nothing was reversed. "Not stated" is incorrect because that admission is written in the second paragraph.

qs.why: The conclusion is two-sided: the scheme remains useful, but its official promise is wrong, so its purpose must be corrected or its map redrawn.
qs.whyOthersFail: The three distractors are actual findings from this study, but each is a single number or proposal, not the conclusion. Half of the trips replacing walking is evidence. Fourteen out of twenty parking spots is an explanation for the cause of that pattern. Moving six spots to the hill is a proposal that, the author says, is only one of two valid paths. The conclusion reads "its stated purpose should be corrected or its map redrawn". The third option is also a summary, but the location of parking spots is the cause of the replacement pattern, not the decision drawn by this study about the scheme's purpose.

qs.why: For five months, they followed 600 registered users and matched new trips with old habits.
qs.whyOthersFail: The method followed 600 registered users for five months and matched new trips with old habits. The number fourteen out of twenty is the location of the docks, emissions are only mentioned as reasoning, and hill residents reported on dock distance, not reasons for walking.

qs.why: The numbers are clearly tiered: nearly half of the trips replaced walking, a quarter replaced minibuses, and only 14 percent replaced motorcycles.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options use the same comparative framework for travel sources, so the text itself acts as the blocker. Minibuses account for only a quarter, so they are not the most frequent. Walking accounts for nearly half compared to 14 percent for motorcycles, so it is far from balanced. And the planner's prediction that riders would abandon motorcycles has not been proven.

qs.why: Only 14 percent of trips replaced motorcycles while nearly half replaced walking, and fourteen out of twenty docks are in flat areas that were already walkable, so the traffic claim has never been truly tested.
qs.whyOthersFail: The 14 percent figure immediately refutes the second option. The report author states “do not recommend closing the scheme”, so the third option contradicts the text. And hill residents reported that “the nearest dock was too far to be convenient”, the opposite of the last option.

qs.why: The text mentions registered users, but never once discusses costs or monthly fees. There is no information on rates, so it is Not stated.
qs.whyOthersFail: "True" requires rate information that is not present. "False" is also incorrect because the text does not deny the existence of fees; it is silent on the matter.

qs.why: The assessment is described as “mixed” and detailed: the choice of play was more daring than wise with seven actors, but the second act and lighting design were real achievements.
qs.whyOthersFail: The three distractors are indeed written in the second and third paragraphs of this review, but each is just a single compliment, a comparison of acts, or a suggestion, not the overall assessment. The scaffolding stage is a technical success. The second act versus the first act is evidence of the gap. Nine actors and twelve weeks is a recommendation for next year. The assessment reads "the honest verdict is mixed, and I offer it as encouragement rather than complaint".

qs.why: The troupe performed with seven actors, and three of them had only joined in August.
qs.whyOthersFail: Eleven is the number required by the script, while nine actors and twelve weeks is a suggestion for next year. The troupe had seven actors and only three were new, and they joined in August.

qs.why: The evidence of ability the author uses is one: the second act, which relies on two characters who are nearly wordless for twelve minutes, kept ninety audience members completely silent.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options are production descriptions that sound like praise, so the text acts as the blocker. The school warehouse loaner costumes were actually “the one element that looked improvised”. The set was built from borrowed scaffolding and grey cloth, not newly purchased wood. And the three new actors joined in August without a single compliment regarding their memorization speed.

qs.why: The two concluding sentences complement each other: volunteer theater gains nothing from indiscriminate praise, and gains a great deal from being told precisely which parts work.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options use the framework “volunteer companies gain from …”, so the content of the conclusion is being tested. Praise merely for attempting something difficult is exactly what is rejected: “earns nothing by being praised indiscriminately”. Switching to an easy play contradicts the recommendation to try the same play again. And the length or tone of the review is never discussed.

qs.why: The text actually suggests the play be performed again next year with more actors and more time, so this claim is the opposite.
qs.whyOthersFail: "True" is wrong because the polarity of the suggestion is reversed. "Not stated" is wrong because the suggestion to repeat the performance is clearly stated.

qs.why: The core objection is the arithmetic of comparison: trading mature trees for saplings “is not a gain but a delay disguised as progress”, so protecting what already exists is more important than announcing new plantings.
qs.whyOthersFail: The three distractors are actual statements from this column, but each is just a supporting figure or a technical step, not the central claim. The one-third of previous campaign trees that died is the basis for the calculation. The four trees on the market street are an example. The obligation to write a justification is the second line of two proposals, not the overarching thesis. The central claim reads "Trading them for saplings is not a gain but a delay disguised as progress".

qs.why: That one-third mortality rate is what makes the trade-off poor: new saplings need ten years to provide shade, and most of them may not survive the first two summers.
qs.whyOthersFail: There is no replacement of four trees on the market street mentioned in the text; rather, their loss is what is not being counted. Saplings are described as “gives almost no shade for a decade”, so the third option directly contradicts the text. And the logging figures have not been published at all; that publication is what the author is requesting.

qs.why: The value of the four trees is proven through their functions: cooling the bus stop, stabilizing the embankment, and housing birds that will not be visited by saplings for twenty years.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options use the opening “they …” and all are descriptions found in the text, so the blocker is which function is used as evidence of value. Tree age is never mentioned as a figure. The trunk circumference threshold is only proposed as a rule, so no rule has been exceeded yet. And the timing of the logging proves the irony of the announcement, not the value of the trees.

qs.why: The reason is stated directly: no one calculates the loss because there is no requirement for anyone to calculate it, while logging figures “is rarely published at all”.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options use the opening “because …” and all are plausible administrative reasons, so the text acts as the blocker. Planting figures are actually announced festively, not quietly once a year. The time of logging is never mentioned as being at night. And the one-third mortality rate belongs to the previous campaign, not as a reason for unrecorded losses.

qs.why: The first proposal is indeed to publish the number of mature trees cut down alongside the number planted. So True.
qs.whyOthersFail: "False" is wrong because no proposition is reversed. "Not stated" is wrong because the proposal is written explicitly.

qs.why: The conclusion has two parts: the region needs both formats and needs them to talk to each other: radio mentions follow-up episodes, podcasts leave one episode a month to the broadcaster.
qs.whyOthersFail: The three distractors are actual descriptions from the second paragraph of this piece, but each is just one advantage or one disadvantage of one channel, not the conclusion. The seven minutes that force editing is an advantage of radio. The forty-minute episode with dialect versions is an advantage of podcasts. Listeners looking for what is already familiar is a disadvantage of podcasts. The conclusion reads "the region needs both formats, and it needs them to talk to each other". The last option is in the form of a conclusion, but it favors one channel; this piece rejects that bias with "Preservation without circulation becomes a locked cupboard. Circulation without preservation becomes a rumour that fades".

qs.why: The podcast is only three years old, adds three segments each month, and nothing is deleted.
qs.whyOthersFail: 1994 and one story per week are radio programs. Podcasts actually store everything, so no episodes are deleted, and forty minutes is a possible duration, not the number of episodes per month.

qs.why: Radio's strengths are mentioned as two: a storyteller with seven minutes must cut content, resulting in a version recognizable to grandparents, and listeners encounter stories they did not choose.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options are phrases describing format advantages, so the text acts as the blocker. Forty-minute long episodes with storyteller explanations and stored dialect versions are podcast advantages, not radio. Free access to familiar stories also belongs to podcasts, and it is precisely from that that “the strange tales are heard least”.

qs.why: The reason is stated in the proposal sentence: the broadcaster's taste is “less predictable than a search box”, whereas a search box only provides what has already been searched for.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options use the opening “because …”, so the reason actually written in the text acts as the blocker. The program's age since 1994 is used to explain radio discipline, not the authority to choose episodes. Recording dialect versions is podcast work. And those who rarely search for foreign stories are podcast listeners, not the radio broadcaster, which is the reason for this proposal.

qs.why: The text mentions the program's age and its rhythm, but never compares the number of listeners over time. That comparison is not made, so it is Not stated.
qs.whyOthersFail: "True" requires listener data that is not present. "False" is also incorrect because the text does not deny that increase; it simply does not measure it.

qs.why: There are two locking signals: "the burden of justification rest with whoever installs them" and the list of demands closed by "demonstrate that losses genuinely decline". The tool is already installed; what the author requests is proof from the party that installed it, not removal and not a single improvement.
qs.whyOthersFail: All three distractors stand on the author's side (suspicious of the surveillance) but are wrong in degree or target, and each has a blocking phrase. Temporary suspension until rules are published is wrong in DEGREE: blocked by "None of this requires that the cameras be removed tomorrow", because the author allows the cameras to stay on while the conditions are met. Emphasis on uneven error rates is wrong in TARGET: blocked by "the cost carried by the thousands of innocent faces measured every hour" and "they are merely the raw material of the method"; the measurement itself is the cost, whereas uneven errors are used only to reject neutral claims, not ranked as the heaviest. Improvement of notice boards is wrong in SCOPE: blocked by the list of four demands "Publish the rules, provide an appeal, delete what is unnecessary, and demonstrate that losses genuinely decline", whereas the door sign is only the start of the observation.

qs.why: The text mentions the list was compiled by a private security firm, not a court, and the standard of proof is determined by the firm itself.
qs.whyOthersFail: The court is actually mentioned as the party that did NOT compile the list; the landlord appears only as the party that approved the camera installation, not the one deciding the names; and shop staff are mentioned as the party facing the risk, without any role in the recording.

qs.why: The conclusion refuses to demand removal ("None of this requires that the cameras be removed tomorrow") while also mentioning "a promise that nobody has audited": not confident in the shopping center's defense, but not asking for the cameras to be dismantled.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options use the same form (uncertain or bothered, then holding back) so the option form no longer points to the key; the selector is the target of that restraint. Handing the appeal process to the firm is wrong in TARGET: the blocking phrases are "provide an appeal" and "Nor is there any independent body to which a complaint might sensibly be addressed". Not demanding loss figures is also wrong in TARGET: the blocking phrase is "demonstrate that losses genuinely decline". Calmness regarding the measurement itself is wrong in NUANCE: the blocking phrase is "the cost carried by the thousands of innocent faces measured every hour".

qs.why: The reduction of losses still stands as a condition that must be met ("demonstrate that losses genuinely decline"), and the condition is only requested for things not yet shown.
qs.whyOthersFail: Hidden measurements are blocked by the phrase "a promise that nobody has audited", not stored, they indeed do not exist yet; occasional audits by the firm that compiled the list are refuted by the same phrase, because what is "convenient" for the firm concerns the list's standard of proof, not the audited loss figures; and the retailer's admission regarding smaller savings has no trace, because the text only speculates that retailers "should welcome such tests".

qs.why: This is a paraphrase: "no reliable route to discovering the fact" means the same as having no reliable way to know.
qs.whyOthersFail: "False" is wrong because the text does not deny this; "Not stated" is wrong because the sentence exists, it just uses different words.

qs.why: Paragraph two mentions the cause as “less dramatic than fraud” then details small samples, freedom of analysis, and journal selection: ordinary weaknesses, not fraud.
qs.whyOthersFail: The self-audit option as the core is limited by the text itself via “in a narrow sense”; the journal option as the main cause clashes with “Journals compounded the problem”, so it adds to rather than precedes; the credibility restored option clashes with “nobody claims the problem is settled”.

qs.why: The reform establishes an order: "Teams now register their predictions and their procedures before gathering data, which makes any later adjustment visible to a reader." Predictions and procedures are registered first, so later adjustments are visible to the reader.
qs.whyOthersFail: Analyzing data first then registering the most suitable predictions REVERSES that order and actually describes the freedom being corrected: "Researchers also enjoyed considerable freedom in how they measured and analysed what they collected." Demanding full replication before publication EXCEEDS the text, because editors accept papers "on the strength of its design alone, before a single result is known". Holding back procedure registration until raw data is released reverses both: raw data is published "alongside the paper itself", not as a prerequisite.

qs.why: The closing sentence of paragraph three praises the results then holds back: "replication rates have improved, though nobody claims the problem is settled". So the agreement is full, the resolution of the problem is rejected.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options agree with the reform and all three reject something, so the "holding back" pattern no longer marks the key; the selector is the target of that rejection. Refusing to admit that the discipline caught itself is wrong in TARGET: the blocking phrase is "the discipline had caught itself out without outside help". Refusing to clear the first researcher of fraud charges is wrong in TARGET and DEGREE: the blocking phrases are "The reasons proved less dramatic than fraud" and "small choices made in good faith". Restriction on changes to publishing methods is wrong in SCOPE: the blocking phrase is "Sample sizes have grown, several laboratories often run the same procedure together".

qs.why: The last sentence mentions the discipline's only asset as "the right to be believed", which is the reason readers still have to trust what is published; that stance is set as a rebuttal to accusations of dampening enthusiasm.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options use the same contrast form ("not X so much as Y") and the same degree of elegance; each distractor shifts EXACTLY ONE element from the source claim. The position among neighboring sciences option shifts SCOPE, from reader trust to interdisciplinary prestige, and is blocked by "the only asset the discipline has, which is the right to be believed". The journal option shifts AGENT: the sentence mentions "Researchers who keep insisting on the point", not journals, which in paragraph two are actually said to have compounded the problem. The quickly restored reputation option shifts TIME and is blocked by "Confidence ought to accumulate slowly, through repetition".

qs.why: The text states the opposite: journals prefer surprising findings over ordinary ones, so the direction of the claim is reversed.
qs.whyOthersFail: "True" directly contradicts that sentence; "Not stated" does not apply because the journal preference is explicitly mentioned.

qs.why: The locking sentence separates two layers: "Neither colleague disputes the arithmetic; their quarrel concerns what marking is for", then the conclusion calls it "a decision about values". So the dispute over the tool is actually about the purpose of grading.
qs.whyOthersFail: Three options use the same "really one about X" frame, so the key is not prominent in form, and all three align with the thesis that the dispute is deeper than the tool. The one pointing to workload is wrong in TARGET: the blocking phrases are "Neither colleague disputes the arithmetic" and the admission "He concedes that the workload problem is real". The one pointing to trust in staff is also wrong in TARGET: the blocking phrase is "their quarrel concerns what marking is for", not the extent to which staff are trusted. Weighing that favors the pragmatic side is wrong in DEGREE: the blocking phrase is "Neither is arguing in bad faith", and the author does not decide.

qs.why: The text mentions examiners now spend weekends on structure and citation formatting.
qs.whyOthersFail: Grading arguments is actually the work they want to reclaim if machines take over technical matters, so it is not the current state; advice on the courage to write is the concern of literature lecturers, not the examiner's task; and a comparison of human values with software values was never reported to have happened.

qs.why: The other three choices are institutional promises or the voice of one of the lecturers; the warning that purchasing decisions could shift the meaning of the work is the author's own assessment.
qs.whyOthersFail: The matter of trained judgment is the argument of the first lecturer quoted by the author, not his opinion; the objection about smooth uniformity belongs to the literature lecturer; and the three-week feedback promise is a departmental promise opened as administrative background.

qs.why: The locking sentence juxtaposes a bold essay that is half-successful with a neat essay that says nothing, and the bold one is said to be able to fall below the other.
qs.whyOthersFail: The generosity of an exhausted examiner is blocked by "a tired marker working towards midnight is not [predictable]"; he is described as hard to predict, not kinder; fluctuating grades clash with "the software is at least predictable", so the problem is the direction of the grade, not its consistency; and the association with the literature lecturer misreads the concession "He concedes that the workload problem is real", which he accepts for the sake of honesty, not because of experimental essays.

qs.why: "Predictable" in the text means the same as unchanging, and that is indeed the reason the first lecturer values it.
qs.whyOthersFail: "False" is wrong because there is no rebuttal; "Not stated" is wrong because that reason is written, just with different word choices.

qs.why: The first paragraph concludes that unpaid credit placements are a burden shifted from employers to students and their sponsors.
qs.whyOthersFail: The university's role as a labor supplier is only conditionally valid in the text (“Where an employer substitutes”) and is not its main claim; the option to remove placements from the degree scheme clashes with “The remedy need not be dramatic” which calls for a stipend; the option of transcripts as the agent shifts the cause, because transcripts merely record achievements without tracking what was affordable.

qs.why: The text separates two things: diaries are graded, but the working hours behind them are rarely checked.
qs.whyOthersFail: Diaries are actually an example of things that are indeed graded; replacing junior positions is mentioned as a consequence the author worries about, not something the university checks; and rent is used to explain who can afford to participate, with no link to inspection.

qs.why: The first paragraph describes the official response coming in "smoothly" and looking "like a gift", then the third sentence reverses it into "a charge quietly transferred": dry, suspicious, without open anger.
qs.whyOthersFail: Three options use the same dry-skeptical tone as the key, so the register no longer distinguishes them; the selectors are the target and nuance. Skepticism toward students taking placements is the wrong TARGET: the blocking phrases are "the credit she forgoes is not optional" and "an applicant filtered by household wealth"; what is questioned is the filter, not those who pass. The doubt that experience must be gained somewhere is the wrong NUANCE: the blocking phrase is "That is true, and it is precisely the difficulty". The factual report option is also the wrong NUANCE: the blocking phrase is "The arrangement looks like a gift", an evaluation rather than a statement.

qs.why: The phrase "the credit she forgoes is not optional" locks in her loss: that credit still appears on the same transcript as that of a student who can afford to participate.
qs.whyOthersFail: University allowances are blocked in their status as a proposal, "universities could require", so they do not yet exist; recruiters' reading of rejections clashes with "Employers... mistake the outcome for merit", because what reaches them is the result of wealth selection, while the rejection is invisible; and repetition in another semester is refuted by the word "not optional", which closes the door on replacement.

qs.why: The nearest sentence merely proposes that the proportion be published, so the figure is not yet in the text; the nature of its absence: quantity is not mentioned.
qs.whyOthersFail: "True" requires a number that was never written; "False" is also wrong because the text does not deny any proportion.

qs.why: The sequence in the final paragraph is the clincher: "officials can dispute a slogan, whereas a table of measurements is more stubborn", followed by the closing about inequality turning into "something a council can be asked to answer for".
qs.whyOthersFail: The three distractors repeat a real part of the text's thesis (street measurement is important), but stop at the finding rather than the author's purpose.
