qs.why: The author does not say the argument is wrong; he says that argument has never been tested by the people who use it most often.
qs.whyOthersFail: The option of a false claim clashes with “The objection is not that the argument is erroneous”; the option of a claim that has been tested clashes with the continuation of that sentence, “it has never been examined by the individuals who make it most often”; the final screen display option adds a point that is not discussed.

qs.why: The text mentions six teams, three locations, and fourteen months, but never says whether they worked simultaneously or in turns. So it is Not stated.

qs.why: “The uneventfulness is the event” artinya justru ketiadaan kejadian itulah kerja rawa: karbon tetap tersimpan selama airnya nggak diganggu.

qs.why: In a hall with reverberation over two seconds, the pause between the final chord and the first clap extends by about four hundred milliseconds. That is exactly the relationship being asked about.

qs.why: The sentence says behavior considered mere convention actually has “a physics” that changes from hall to hall. So it means measurable regularity imposed by the room, not a branch of science.
qs.whyOthersFail: The branch of science option uses the most common meaning of “physics”, whereas the next sentence explains it as “the physics changes from hall to hall”; the microphone arrangement option is the measurement tool, not the regularity being measured; the reverberation time formula option narrows it to one quantity, whereas the text uses it for room behavior regarding applause.

qs.why: The text only says all four are in cities with similar concert habits, and that the halls are European. The country is not mentioned at all, so it is Not stated.
qs.whyOthersFail: “True” requires a statement of the country which is absent. “False” also requires proof that the countries are different, and that is equally absent.

qs.why: The key sentence says the belief collapsed not because the science was wrong, but because its rhetoric promised more than the science ever offered.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options open with the same thesis, so the thesis guessed from other questions is not enough and the second clause must be read. The option of removing recommendations is refuted by “Nothing about stating a range requires abandoning a recommendation”; the option of straightforward verbs is refuted by “lay audiences handle stated ranges tolerably well”; the option of a fault in the science is refuted by “the genuine fault was rhetorical”.

qs.why: The two fields of study cited show that laypeople are quite capable of reading ranges. So the assumption that the public is incapable is actually not supported by evidence.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options call it an assumption, so the form does not mark the key. The option of studies confirming it is refuted by “lay audiences handle stated ranges tolerably well”; the option of negating instructions is refuted by “A warning can specify a seventy per cent chance and still instruct everybody to leave”; the option of applying only to prognosis is refuted by the word “both” in “Studies of flood warnings and of medical prognosis both indicate”.

qs.why: Penulis nyebut keberatan itu “a serious argument deserving better than the slogan it has become”. Diakui seriusnya, ditolak wujudnya sekarang.
qs.whyOthersFail: The option of an objection invented without evidence conflicts with “This is a serious argument”; the option of reasons to keep sentences firm conflicts with the next sentence, which states that ranges and instructions work at different levels; the option of risk being worsened by ranges conflicts with the example of a seventy percent warning that still orders evacuation.

qs.why: What the practitioner defends are the two translations in the first paragraph: distribution into one number, then a number into one verb. So the word means the condensation of complex findings into a brief statement.
qs.whyOthersFail: All four options are concise definitions of equal precision, three being for other meanings of the word. The option of air compression uses its physical meaning; the option of a quarterly horizon uses the recession example from paragraph three; the option of broadcast cutting uses the “fourteen seconds” figure from paragraph one, whereas what is compressed is the findings, namely “converts a distribution into a number”.

qs.why: The last sentence calls the habit rational, even if it is expensive to dismantle. Rational and reasonable are equivalent here, so it is True.
qs.whyOthersFail: “False” requires the author to call it irrational, and he does not. “Not stated” fails because the assessment is explicit.

qs.why: The text states that the omission is a result of a format chosen for economic reasons, then maintained as tradition. The brass plaque is concise because a brief text is approved without delay.

qs.whyOthersFail: The more durable laminated sheet option contradicts “It is ugly and will not survive the season”; the board rejecting it due to lack of durability contradicts the reason given in the conclusion, which is that the sheet proves the format is a decision; the board adopting it contradicts “It will not, of course”.

qs.why: The text says the length only summoned a second committee, and the second committee produced the same prose at additional expense. That is dry skepticism, not a proposal.

Resignation is ruled out because the author says one clause would achieve more and asks for the laminated sheet to be made standard. And annoyance at the conservation officer is ruled out because he only appears as one of the format's requirements.

qs.why: The sentence says the adjective performs “the labour of an absent fact”: work that should have been done by a fact that was not included.
qs.whyOthersFail: The factory labor and street market trade options both use the meaning of “labour” as human work, whereas the sentence mentions “an adjective performing the labour of an absent fact”; the committee's effort to approve the text shifts the actor to the committee, not the adjective.

qs.why: The text says the sheet is not a partner to the city council, and the next sentence mentions “somebody” who attached it. So the claim is false.
qs.whyOthersFail: “True” directly contradicts the sentence. “Not stated” fails because the author explicitly states its origin.

qs.why: The author says the value is not in the content, but in how certainty sounds when that certainty is almost proven wrong.
qs.whyOthersFail: The reliable source on atoms option contradicts “it would be imprudent to attempt it”; the incompetent compilers option contradicts “The compilers were not obtuse; they were early”; the supplement maintaining currency option contradicts “That belief is now unavailable”.

qs.why: The text says the possibility of continental drift has not yet reached a position where it can be rejected. This means the question does not yet exist, not that it has been answered incorrectly.

qs.why: The text says the habit scores points off the dead who cannot revise, and flatters the reader with a superiority they did not earn.

qs.why: The text says a hedge needs an opponent: you only install a barrier if there is a counter-position. So it means a hedging phrase that softens a claim.
qs.whyOthersFail: The confident statement option reverses the meaning, as the sentence reads “The prose contains no hedge, since a hedge requires an opponent”; the supplement option uses the subject of paragraph five, not this word; the row of plants option uses the most common dictionary meaning of “hedge” which is unrelated to prose.

qs.why: The sentence calls the loss of confidence a real loss as well as a correction. The claim just rearranges that sentence, so it is True.

qs.whyOthersFail: The better baseline option contradicts “improved baselines will not resolve a category error”; the beauty and obligation option that collects more reverses “raised considerably less money”; the annual audit of airlines uses the detail from paragraph three as a proposal, whereas it is only a marker of asymmetry.

qs.why: The text says defenders of the mechanism “are entitled to” point at the intact canopy and ask how strong the objection actually is.
qs.whyOthersFail: The exaggerating option contradicts “Defenders of the mechanism are entitled to point at intact canopy”; the misled by accountants option shifts the target, as accountants are only mentioned as recorders; the irrelevant option contradicts “the alternative is not obviously preferable”.

qs.stem: Why is Molen hiding behind the flower pot?
options: He wants to eat the flowers.
He is afraid of the loud noise.
He is looking for his cage.
qs.why: Molen hid right after hearing a noisy car, so he was startled and afraid of that sound.
qs.whyOthersFail: The text does not say Molen ate flowers, was tired, or was looking for a cage; what happened before he hid was the sound of a car.

qs.stem: What can we conclude about Molen?
options: Molen does not play outside all day.
Molen sleeps on the grass at night.
Molen opens his cage door by himself.
Molen eats grass in the morning.
qs.why: The cage was only opened in the afternoon and Molen went back to sleep in the cage, so he did not play outside all day.
qs.whyOthersFail: Molen slept in the cage, not on the grass; it was Ragil who opened the cage; the morning activity described is Ragil feeding Molen, not Molen eating grass in the garden.

qs.stem: In the text, what does the word “it” in “Ragil laughs and gives it a carrot” refer to?
qs.why: The one given a carrot was certainly Molen, the rabbit that had just hidden in the previous sentence.
qs.whyOthersFail: Flower pots, cars, and cages are not creatures that can be fed carrots and are not the subjects being discussed.

qs.stem: What is this text about?
options: a girl who buys a new cage
a boy and his pet rabbit
qs.why: All sentences tell the story of Ragil and his rabbit Molen: playing, hiding, eating a carrot, then sleeping.
qs.whyOthersFail: Flowers were just a hiding place, the car was only heard, and no one bought a new cage.

qs.stem: What does Ragil give to Molen?
qs.why: The text states directly: Ragil gave Molen a carrot.
qs.whyOthersFail: Flowers and grass were just places for Molen to play and hide; toys are not mentioned in the text.

qs.stem: What can we conclude about the kite when the wind is strong?
options: The kite is easy to hold with one hand.
The kite is not easy to hold.
The kite falls to the ground quickly.
The kite is too heavy to fly.
qs.why: Andi had to hold the string with both hands because the kite was pulling hard, meaning it was not easy to hold.
qs.whyOthersFail: Two hands were used precisely because one hand was not enough; the kite was flying high, not falling, and it clearly could fly.

qs.stem: In the text, what does the word “it” in “Many children look at it” refer to?
qs.why: The previous sentence describes the kite flying high, so 'it' refers to Andi's kite that the children were watching.
qs.whyOthersFail: The field and the wind are not things that were rising and attracting attention, and Andi's uncle was not being discussed in that sentence.

qs.stem: In the text, what does “high” mean?
qs.why: Strong wind made the kite fly far up into the sky; that is the meaning of 'high' here.
qs.whyOthersFail: 'high' is the opposite of near the ground; the text also does not say the kite was slow, heavy, or in the water.

qs.stem: Who went to the field with Andi?
qs.why: The text states directly: Andi went to a large field with his uncle.
qs.whyOthersFail: Father, teacher, and sister are not mentioned in the text; the one accompanying him is 'his uncle'.

qs.stem: What is this text about?
options: a boy who bought a new bag
an uncle who works in the fields
a boy who is flying his new kite
qs.why: The text follows Andi and his new kite from home until it flies high in the field.
qs.whyOthersFail: There is no new bag or soccer ball, and his uncle accompanied Andi, rather than working in the field.

qs.stem: How does Ilham feel about his new haircut?
options: He wants his hair to be long again.
He is afraid of the mirror.
qs.why: Ilham looked in the mirror and then said thank you, a sign that he liked the result of his haircut.
qs.whyOthersFail: People who are angry or disappointed do not say thank you, and the text does not show that he was afraid of the mirror.

qs.stem: In the text, who does the word "they" in "they wait on a long seat" refer to?
qs.why: The people who came to the barbershop were Ilham and his father, so they were the ones waiting.
qs.whyOthersFail: The barber was working, not waiting; Ilham did not come with the barber; people at home are not in the story.

qs.stem: In the text, what does "busy" mean?
qs.why: Because the shop was 'busy', they had to wait, meaning the shop was full of people.
qs.whyOthersFail: If the shop were closed, they could not wait inside; cold or cleanliness does not make people have to queue.

qs.stem: When did Ilham go to the barber?
qs.why: The text states the time directly: Sunday morning.
qs.whyOthersFail: Friday, Monday night, and Tuesday are not mentioned in the text at all.

qs.stem: What did Ilham do after getting a haircut?
options: He waited on the long bench.
He washed his hair at home.
qs.why: After getting a haircut, Ilham looked in the mirror and said thank you.
qs.whyOthersFail: Waiting in the chair happened before the haircut, and the text does not mention a new comb or washing hair at home.

qs.stem: What can we conclude about the students now?
options: They are still very afraid of the box.
They want the box to be moved.
They touch the bees every day.
They are not as afraid as before.
qs.why: The phrase 'At first' shows the fear was only at the beginning; after knowing the bees were calm, that fear decreased.
qs.whyOthersFail: 'At first ... but' marks a change, so 'still very afraid' contradicts the text; there was no request to move the box, and the bees were calm specifically 'when nobody touches the box'.

qs.stem: What can we understand about the honey?
options: The school sells honey every month.
The school does not have the honey yet.
The bees ate all the honey in May.
Mrs. Ratna bought honey at the market.
qs.why: The first honey will only come in June, so the school does not have the honey yet.
qs.whyOthersFail: 'first honey' means there has never been honey for sale; the text does not mention bees finishing the honey or Mrs. Ratna buying honey.

qs.stem: In the last sentence, whose possession does the word "its" refer to?
qs.why: 'its' is attached to 'the school' in the same sentence: the first honey belongs to the school.
qs.whyOthersFail: The beehive and science room are not the parties that 'will get' the honey; the recipient of the honey is the school, not Mrs. Ratna personally.

qs.stem: In the text, what does “calm” mean?
qs.why: The opposite of the students' fear: the bees are calm and will not attack as long as the hive is not touched.
qs.whyOthersFail: Words that calm students cannot mean fast and noisy, hungry, or big and heavy.

qs.stem: What is this text mainly about?
options: a teacher who sells flowers at school
a school that keeps bees in small boxes
students who are installing a new fence
a class that cooks with honey
qs.why: All sentences describe the beehive at school: who installed it, how the bees are, and the honey being awaited.
qs.whyOthersFail: Flowers are just where bees forage, the fence is only mentioned in passing, and there is no cooking activity yet; the honey does not even exist yet.

qs.stem: What can we understand about the capacity for Star Night?
options: Everyone in town can come without registering.
The office sells tickets on Saturday.
Not everyone will get a spot.
Only teachers are allowed to register.
qs.why: If the space is limited and requires prior registration, it means not everyone will get a spot.
qs.whyOthersFail: You must write your name before Friday, so you cannot just show up; the event is free, so no tickets are sold; there are no special rules for teachers.

qs.stem: What can we conclude about the telescope?
options: The school bought two new telescopes.
Mr. Surya works in the school administration office.
The science club meets every Saturday.
The telescope was brought by a guest.
qs.why: The telescope was brought by Mr. Surya from the city science club, who is a guest from outside the school.
qs.whyOthersFail: Mr. Surya brought the telescope, the school did not buy it; Mr. Surya is from a city club, not a school office employee; the club's routine schedule is not mentioned.

qs.stem: In the text, what does the word “it” in “it is a good month to start” refer to?
qs.why: 'it' is referred to as 'a good month', so it refers to the month of July, not another object.
qs.whyOthersFail: The moon in the sky, the field, and the Star Night event are not a 'month', so they do not fit the phrase 'a good month' in that sentence.

qs.stem: What time does Star Night start?
qs.why: The announcement clearly states: seven o'clock in the evening.
qs.whyOthersFail: Five, nine, and six in the morning do not appear in the announcement.

qs.stem: Why is the school making this announcement?
options: to close the school field at night
to request funds for the science club
to invite people to a stargazing night
qs.why: This announcement invites people to come to the stargazing event: it includes an invitation 'Come', the time, and how to register.
qs.whyOthersFail: The telescope was brought to be used, not sold; the field was opened for the event; the event is free, so it is not about making money.

qs.stem: What can we conclude about the salt production?
options: It takes days of hot sun.
It is faster during the rainy season.
The process takes place in a large factory.
It requires cold seawater at night.
qs.why: Seawater must be dried for days and the hot sun is what dries it, so salt production requires many sunny days.
qs.whyOthersFail: Rain actually stops the work, so the rainy season does not speed it up; the location is an open field near the sea, not a factory; the hot sun does the work, not cold water at night.

qs.stem: In the text, who does the word “He” in “He makes salt” refer to?
qs.why: The previous sentence mentions Nadia's uncle in Madura, so 'He' is her uncle.
qs.whyOthersFail: The workers are mentioned later, Nadia's father does not appear in the text, and there are no salt sellers in the story.

qs.stem: In the text, what does “collect” mean?
qs.why: The workers take and gather salt from the ground using wooden tools; that is what 'collect' means.
qs.whyOthersFail: Salt is collected, not thrown into the sea; washing salt with water would dissolve it; selling is not done with long wooden tools.

qs.stem: Why does the work stop when the rain comes?
options: because the seawater is too cold
because the field must remain dry
because the tools are damaged by the rain
qs.why: The reason is written directly: the salt field must remain dry.
qs.whyOthersFail: The text does not mention workers being tired, seawater temperature, or broken tools; the reason is only about the field needing to be dry.

qs.stem: What is this text mainly about?
options: how salt is made by the seaside
how rain helps the salt field
qs.why: The text explains the sequence of making salt: seawater is dried, it evaporates, then the salt is collected.
qs.whyOthersFail: Nadia visited, she did not swim; wooden tools are used to collect salt, not to make boats; rain actually stops the work.

qs.why: The previous sentence describes turtles laying eggs in warm sand, so 'those eggs' are the eggs left by the turtles on the beach.
qs.whyOthersFail: Eggs sold at the market are only a small part of the final outcome, not the reference for that phrase; dogs dig up nests, they do not bring eggs to the beach; the fenced corner at the post only appeared in the last two years, not 'for a long time'.

qs.why: 'this' summarizes the thing just mentioned in the same sentence: school children coming to watch.
qs.whyOthersFail: Selling eggs is actually the problem the group is fighting against; there is no plan to move the post; marking nests is indeed their job, but it is not the thing just mentioned before the word 'this'.

qs.why: Their subsequent activities explain the meaning: walking at night, marking nests, and moving eggs to keep them safe, which is protecting.
qs.whyOthersFail: There is no beach cleaning activity; children are actually allowed to come, so the beach is not closed; selling eggs is what they are fighting against.

qs.why: Enam puluh satu sarang itu hampir dua kali angka tahun pertama, jadi hasil kerja kelompok ini meningkat.
qs.whyOthersFail: 'almost twice' means the results are very different, not the same; they are clearly still counting because the numbers exist; what is being counted are the protected nests, not the number of turtles that arrive.

qs.why: The core of the article is the group of fishermen protecting the beach: marking nests, moving eggs, and escorting hatchlings to the sea.
qs.whyOthersFail: Children are only watching, not learning to swim; dogs are just one of the threats in the opening paragraph; the market is mentioned briefly as an old problem.

qs.why: 'she' continues the name just mentioned in that sentence, Mrs. Halimah; she heard Yusuf's answer from the next row.
qs.whyOthersFail: The customer asking could not possibly 'hear from the next row' their own conversation; Yusuf's mother is not in the text; other workers are never mentioned.

qs.why: The customer came with a photo without the plant's name, so what Yusuf learned was to recognize plants upon seeing them.
qs.whyOthersFail: Watering was his other first task, not the meaning of this word; Yusuf did not buy plants for the shop; planting in pots is not mentioned at all.

qs.why: Mrs. Halimah smiled precisely after hearing Yusuf answer for himself, a sign she was satisfied with Yusuf's progress.
qs.whyOthersFail: A smile is not a sign of anger; the text does not say whether the customer ended up buying; if the answer were wrong, Mrs. Halimah's smile would not make sense and the text would certainly mention her correction.

qs.why: His plan is stated clearly: to continue studying agriculture after graduating.
qs.whyOthersFail: Bus fare is just his expense, not his ambition; he is actually getting closer to plants; mathematics is never mentioned.

qs.why: Yusuf's initial tasks are stated directly: watering seedlings before the sun gets hot and sweeping the path between the tables.
qs.whyOthersFail: Serving customers and the leaf notebook came after a month; carrying plants to the bus stop is not in the text.

qs.why: The following sentences contain good news (84 percent of glasses returned, trash bins rarely full), so 'encouraging' means giving hope.
qs.whyOthersFail: The numbers are actually presented neatly, so they are not difficult to calculate or impossible to check; the subsequent news is positive, not smaller than expected.

qs.why: Trash bins that previously had to be emptied three times a day were clearly full to the point of overflowing; that is 'overflow'.
qs.whyOthersFail: The trash bin remains there, it is not missing; odors and wind are not mentioned in the text; the clue is about the frequency of emptying, so the meaning is about being full.

qs.why: The previous sentence reads 'The office concludes...', so 'Its' continues the same subject: the student environmental office that conducted the trial.
qs.whyOthersFail: The library is only the proposed location for a new return point; the cafe is the party receiving the recommendation, not the one giving it; the university is never the subject that concludes.

qs.why: Closing just one counter caused returns at the other two counters to drop within days; a small obstacle immediately lowered the return numbers.
qs.whyOthersFail: The text does not compare old and new counters; the library does not yet have a return point; what dropped was returns, not missing glasses.

qs.why: That sentence mentions the savings as well as the reason: washing returned glasses is cheaper than buying new paper cups.
qs.whyOthersFail: Trash bins that are rarely full is a matter of cleanliness, not cafe money; the 84 percent figure indicates compliance, not savings; customers who refuse the deposit are actually the weak point of the scheme.

qs.why: What was shrinking and causing Wulan to look for a solution was her daily income; this is reinforced by another sentence that 'sales have risen by a third' after she broadcasted.
qs.whyOthersFail: Baskets and stock are not described as shrinking slowly; customers are described as aging, and that is distinguished from 'takings' by the word 'and' in the same sentence.

qs.why: The person the merchant is talking to during the broadcast is her phone, the object that is the initial subject of that sentence.
qs.whyOthersFail: The tripod is just a phone stand; the queue is currently being served, distinguished by the word 'while'; the market aisle cannot be talked to in the context of a broadcast.

qs.why: 'It' continues the subject of the previous sentence, 'The market cooperative', the party that installed lights and opened night classes.
qs.whyOthersFail: Night classes are actually one of the things run by 'It'; the middle aisle is where the lights were installed; Mr. Hasan is actually a merchant who gave up, not the one who installed the lights.

qs.why: 'flatters vegetables' means vegetables look better than they actually are, and 'hides a fish's condition' means the state of the fish cannot be judged through a screen.
qs.whyOthersFail: The camera actually makes vegetables look better, not worse; according to Mr. Hasan, the camera hides the fish's condition, so the fish does not benefit; what must be smelled directly according to him is the fish, not the vegetables.

qs.why: This article captures an old market that has started selling via live broadcasts: the pioneers, those who refuse, and the cooperative's middle-ground stance.
qs.whyOthersFail: There is no comparison of fish and vegetable earnings; the cooperative actually 'refuses to make broadcasting a requirement'; no kiosks are closed in the text.

qs.why: 'it' continues the subject of that sentence itself: 'The gap between those two numbers', which is referred to as a hidden subsidy.
qs.whyOthersFail: The officer in the orange vest is only a money intermediary; asphalt is the land being contested, not the thing that 'distorts'; shop rental price is only one of the two numbers forming 'the gap'.

qs.why: 'this cruising' points back to the activity just described at the beginning of the sentence: drivers circling around looking for an empty spot.
qs.whyOthersFail: Buses and couriers are never mentioned in the text; pedestrians appear only through the word 'pavement' as the party losing space, not as a source of congestion.

qs.why: Because the tariff is too small to have an effect, the price stops working as a filter; the space is then contested through luck. The first paragraph gives the scale: two thousand rupiah for land worth millions.
qs.whyOthersFail: The issue of receipts is only implied by the orange vest in another paragraph, not the meaning of this word; 'flat' actually means the tariff is uniform, and no national law is mentioned.

qs.why: If there are fewer car-driving customers than the merchant expected, and the biggest spenders actually arrive on foot or by public transport, then the losses from realistic pricing are smaller than feared.
qs.whyOthersFail: The text refers to counting customers, not installing meters; 'overestimate' means a miscalculation, not an intentional lie; the biggest spenders are those arriving without cars, not mall visitors.

qs.why: The author explicitly rejects hostility toward drivers and concludes with measurable technical proposals: pricing, transparent meters, and visible shopping.
qs.whyOthersFail: The evidence sentence actually refutes a hostile stance toward drivers; there is no nostalgia for the pre-car era; the position is very clear (the curb should be valued as public land), so it is not indecisive.

qs.why: The previous sentence mentions the project was reported 'as an act of rescue', and the author distinguishes that word from the work itself, so it is the word 'rescue' that is annoying.
qs.whyOthersFail: 'archive' is only discussed several sentences later; 'project' is actually part of 'the work itself' which the author accepts; 'recording' is the activity, while the issue is the rescue label attached to that activity.

qs.why: The previous sentence reads 'Nobody holding a marketing degree designed these sounds', and 'They' refers back to 'these sounds', which are the merchants' signal sounds.
qs.whyOthersFail: A marketing degree is mentioned only to be dismissed as a designer; rival merchants and zinc roofs are just part of the list of problems solved by the sounds, not things 'refined by use'.

qs.why: The previous paragraph describes the sound as a call that 'demanded a decision, sandals or no sandals'; that is the 'summons', a call demanding an answer, and that is what dies along with its context.
qs.whyOthersFail: Food prices are never discussed; recording quality is actually what survives in the archive; the vendor's route is only implied by 'faded past the neighbour's gate' and is not what is contrasted with 'craftsmanship'.

qs.why: Throughout the essay, the author separates two things: the sound can be saved, but its summoning power (which once interrupted your night and demanded a decision) is not; 'A recording in an archive interrupts nobody'.
qs.whyOthersFail: The sentence about recordings being 'clean, catalogued, and searchable' is ironic; those qualities are described as things the original sound lacked, not improvements; a recording 'interrupts nobody' while the original sound demands a decision, so they are not equivalent; what displaces the sound is delivery apps, not the archive.

qs.why: Penulis menolak meromantisir perubahan dan menyebut dua keuntungan nyatanya: makanannya tetap sampai, dan penjual nggak lagi berjalan berjam-jam kehujanan.
qs.whyOthersFail: There is no call to ban apps; the taste of the soup is never mentioned; 'the same soup' actually implies the soup is the same; and the text only mentions the direction of change ('grow rarer each year') without predicting the sound's return.
